summary.prose: Story s9 moves the last direct git and gh calls of the workflow library, the daemon, the analyze path, the identity lookup and the design corpus reader onto the registry's typed tools, then deletes the old paths that s10 left in place (runGit, runGitAsync, runGh, commitAndPushArtifacts, the github.ts wrappers, createGitRunner, the exec test seam) and turns the forbidden-spawn scan to failing mode. Each site calls a named git tool through callTool, keeps its own fallback for an ordinary failure and lets a denial through to the stage boundary, as s10 does. The synchronous sites and the chain above them become async; the team policy reader becomes async, and the refresh's 10 second budget becomes an abort signal plus a per-call time limit.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Alternative a1: the executor in src/daemon/tools/executor.ts becomes the one pipeline for all external operations, and git, gh and Jira (acli) are registry tool families with an optional declared output schema and an approval class (none, common or destructive). Workflow and daemon code call tools through a typed helper that takes the tool definition; about 32 production files that spawn git or gh, or call a wrapper that does, move onto it in one change.

boundary.internal: Private implementation of s9: Move the workflow library's and the daemon's direct git and gh calls onto the registry

adjacentBoundaries.internal: The hook stage inside executeTool: the registry of hooks keyed by tool id, registration order, the rule that a hook runs only after a successful, checked call, and the way a hook failure is carried on the result. It places its stage at step 5 of the pipeline order in the architecture shape and does not own the schema check or the approval step.

The optional output-schema field and the check at step 4 of the pipeline, the typed call helper that takes a tool definition, the serial conversion queue, the key-value cross-check and the one-time escalation, and the shared failure kinds. It includes the choice of schema language and the way an input-to-tool mismatch is reported. It does not declare or read the approval class.

The approval step at step 2 of the pipeline: the single approval field on a tool definition, the global approval setting for the common class and its default, the IPC request and answer methods, the timeout value, the daemon-side holder of the pending requests, the terminal-client, editor and chat implementations of the answer, and removal of the 'auto-approving' fallback in executor.ts. It maps every existing requiresApproval flag, in every family, to the common class, and lists the tools that change. It does not choose which individual git, gh or Jira operations are destructive; each family Story marks its own.

The list of git operation families, their input and output schemas, which git operations are in the destructive class (for example force push, hard reset, clean, deleting a branch or tag), and the parsing of git porcelain output. Operations that need approval but cannot destroy work stay in the common class. Existing git ids keep their meaning.

The list of gh operation families, their schemas (read from gh --json where it exists, converted from text otherwise, for example gh pr diff and gh run view --log), which of the 27 gh operations that need approval are in the destructive class, and the 120 second time limit and its message. Existing gh ids keep their meaning.

The Jira tool families over acli (work item view, search, create, edit, transition, assign, comment, link, project list and view), their schemas, the --yes flag on every mutating command, the bounded forms of search and project list that acli requires, the 'acli jira auth status' sign-in check, and which operations are in the destructive class. An operation acli does not offer is left out and named as unsupported.

The repository check that fails on a direct git, gh or acli spawn outside src/daemon/tools, built first; the inventory it produces (about 32 production files known today, with the indexer, the design corpus reader, the analyze ignore filter, the understanding identity lookup and the daemon self-update included and no allowlist); the rewrite of every listed site and of the tests that import the old wrappers onto the typed helper; and the removal of runGit, commitAndPushArtifacts and the github.ts wrappers. It keeps the artifacts, commits and tracker records the same as before.
Private implementation of s8: Reach the rest of git through named, typed tools
Private implementation of s10: Move the tracker and the terminal client onto the registry and remove the old paths

nonFunctional.performance: Each gh job has its own time limit from a table keyed by tool id and op, never shorter than the tool has today: reads 30 s (gh_pr_diff and gh_run_view 60 s, searches 60 s), changes 30 s by default, gh_issue_create 60 s, gh_pr_create 90 s, gh_pr_merge and gh_release_create 180 s, gh_repo_create and gh_repo_fork 120 s, downloads and uploads 300 s, gh_repo_clone 600 s, codespace create and rebuild 600 s (decided with the user on 2026-10-25; the daemon is expected to become multi-threaded so a slow gh will not block it). A timed-out call names the command and the limit, and a changing call adds that its outcome is unknown. The approval wait has its own timeout, set in s3's LLD. Conversion is serial, so a text-only tool that needs the cheap model costs one model call per attempt plus at most one escalated call; structured-output tools make no model call.
nonFunctional.security: No argument, setting, environment variable or caller identity can skip the approval for a destructive call; with no client attached the call is denied. Common calls follow one global setting. Approval requests travel only over the daemon's Unix socket. No credentials are read or stored: gh, git and acli use the user's own CLI sessions. A tool that declares an output schema and returns a result that does not match it fails and its result is not passed on. Today the executor runs every tool flagged requiresApproval as approved (11 git tools, 5 more by predicate, 27 gh operations and other families), so nothing asks; this Epic makes destructive calls ask every time and puts the rest under the global setting.
nonFunctional.observability: The executor logs each stage per call with the tool id, the caller, the approval class and decision and its reason, the schema check result, and each hook outcome. Hook failures, denials and conversion escalations are returned to the caller as part of the result, not only logged.
nonFunctional.durability: Pending approval requests are held in memory by the daemon and are lost on restart; a request left open at restart is treated as denied. Hooks are registered in code at start-up, not stored. The global approval setting is stored in the daemon's config. The cutover leaves artifacts, commits and tracker records unchanged.

errors.condition: a git read was denied (no client, declined, timed out, cancelled): thrown, not turned into a failed policy result

api.name: createDeadline
api.signature: export function createDeadline(totalMs?: number, now?: () => number): Deadline

parameters.name: totalMs
parameters.purpose: the total budget; REFRESH_DEADLINE_MS (10 s) by default

dataModelChanges.details: Both result shapes are removed with their runners. The 'quiet' flag (git exited non-zero with no message) maps to the tool failure kind rejected with an empty message; the 'timedOut' flag maps to the tool failure kind timed-out or an aborted deadline signal. The denial reasons are declined, timed-out, no-client and cancelled and arrive as a thrown ToolDenied; there is no 'cancelled' tool failure kind.

Gains `signal: AbortSignal` and `dispose()`. It moves to src/workflow/team/sighting-store.ts beside REFRESH_DEADLINE_MS (git-async.ts is deleted). Each tool call takes timeoutMs = Math.max(1, remainingMs()) and the deadline's signal; when the budget is spent the signal aborts, the running call ends, and the next call is not started because the helper checks remainingMs() first.

PolicyReader returns a Promise. The 44 test files that inject a synchronous reader keep working during the change because the call sites `await` the reader (awaiting a plain value is harmless), and are tightened to async fakes at the end. The envelope PolicyResult is unchanged.

dataModelChanges.details: One row per site, each naming the file and function, the git or gh tool and op, the site's error policy (fallback for an ordinary failure; ToolDenied thrown) and the registry test that runs it against a stand-in git or gh binary. A case where no tool op matches exactly is raised at the start of the build task (t1 verifies every row against the tool's input schema) and is an additive extension of that tool, made inside this Story and flagged for the tool's owner, as s10 did for git_push configured. This Story builds them, as s7 did for git_config, git_ls_remote, git_update_ref and git_rm: new read-only tools git_diff_tree and git_merge_tree, an optional type input on git_hash_object and an optional gitPath input on git_rev_parse, each with its own tests, and the s8 coverage table marks the two tools built by s9.

Removed with the wrappers. The 32 test files that import them are moved to the stand-in git and gh binaries (installStandInBin, installFakeGh) and to injected port fakes; tests that need a recorded executor use the stand-in binary's call log. A helper module for the stand-in gh in tests replaces the legacy table.

errorCases.scenario: A moved site's call is denied (no client attached, declined, approval timed out, or cancelled)
errorCases.detection: callTool returns a failure of kind 'denied' with the denial reason; the helper turns it into a thrown ToolDenied via errorOfFailure (src/workflow/tracker/tool-denied.ts), and no catch-all on the way catches it (isToolDenied is checked before any fallback)
errorCases.response: The calling stage fails with the denial reported (tool id and reason); no later call of the stage is made. The policy reader, the build-start stamp, the range-base reads and the corpus reader let it through to the stage boundary (the gate, the build step, the daemon method), which reports it as the stage's error
errorCases.userImpact: The user sees which tool was denied and why (for example 'git_cat_file was denied: no-client'); nothing is half-written because every site reads or writes after its last call

errorCases.scenario: A git read fails for an ordinary reason (not a work tree, unknown revision, git missing, empty output where a sha was expected)
errorCases.detection: the tool result is a failure of kind rejected, missing-tool or unreachable, or a successful result whose payload says 'not found'; the git-calls helper maps it to undefined or to GitCallFailed carrying the kind and message
errorCases.response: Each site keeps the fallback it has today: the policy reader returns its failed PolicyResult with the same reason text; findAnchor returns its failure; resolveStoryRangeBase returns undefined; headFullSha returns undefined; defaultGitUserName falls back to the OS user; createRepoIgnoreFilter degrades to the permissive filter with its warning

errorCases.scenario: The team policy refresh runs past its 10 second budget
errorCases.detection: createDeadline's timer aborts its AbortSignal when REFRESH_DEADLINE_MS elapses; every call also takes timeoutMs from remainingMs(), and the helper checks remainingMs() before starting a call
errorCases.response: The running call is aborted through deps.signal (the executor kills the process group, settled within 2 s); the refresh returns the same failure as today ('did not finish within the refresh deadline') and starts no call after it; the deadline is disposed in a finally
errorCases.userImpact: The same failure text as today; the sighting lock is never held longer than the 10 s the lock-lifetime reasoning assumes

errorCases.scenario: The refresh's outer signal is aborted (the daemon method is cancelled or the connection closes)
errorCases.detection: the signal passed in opts.signal is combined with the deadline signal; the executor returns a 'denied' failure with denial 'cancelled' for the aborted call
errorCases.response: The cancelled denial is thrown as ToolDenied reason 'cancelled' and ends the refresh at the first call; no further git call starts and the sighting lock is released by the existing finally
errorCases.userImpact: The refresh reports it was cancelled; the policy cache is unchanged

errorCases.scenario: A tool's output does not fit its declared schema, or a text-only tool needs conversion and conversion fails
errorCases.detection: callTool returns a failure of kind schema-mismatch or conversion-failed (the s2 contract)
errorCases.response: Thrown as a GitCallFailed with that kind; it is never turned into a fallback value, so a wrong payload is not passed on (k2). The one exception is a site whose old code already treated every failure as 'absent' (createRepoIgnoreFilter): there the failure is logged and the permissive filter is used, as today
errorCases.userImpact: A stage that depends on the value fails with the tool's message instead of acting on bad data

errorCases.scenario: A site that was synchronous is called by code that still treats the result as a value
errorCases.detection: the compiler: the call's type is Promise and the use does not compile; and the compiler-API no-floating-promises scan from s10 extended to the new helpers, which flags a dropped promise statement
errorCases.response: The build task fixes the caller in the same change; the scan runs in the test suite and the full sweep
errorCases.userImpact: None at run time; the failure is at build time

errorCases.scenario: The scan in failing mode finds a direct spawn or wrapper call outside the exemptions
errorCases.detection: node scripts/forbidden-spawn-scan.mjs --fail exits 1 and lists the site; it exits 2 if a file cannot be parsed
errorCases.response: The build chain fails (package.json build runs the scan with --fail); the site is moved or, if it is a real exemption, added to EXEMPT with its reason in a reviewed change
errorCases.userImpact: None for users; the build breaks for a developer who adds a direct spawn

errorCases.scenario: A test that used the exec seam is left on the removed seam
errorCases.detection: the TypeScript import of _setTrackerExecForTests or the legacy table no longer resolves, and the old-paths test (now inverted) asserts the exports are gone
errorCases.response: Each of the 32 files is moved onto the stand-in git or gh binary or an injected fake in the same change

edgeCases.input: A repository with no remote, no upstream or a detached HEAD
edgeCases.expected: The policy reader, the signoff branch checks and the handoff checks give the same results as today (a failed PolicyResult or 'none', a rejected branch check); each of these is one tool call with the same failure mapping
findAnchor reads isShallow through git_rev_parse and returns the same 'shallow' failure as today without walking history

edgeCases.input: A file name with spaces, newlines or non-UTF-8 bytes in a listing (git ls-files -z today)
edgeCases.expected: git_ls_files returns the paths without losing any (the tool parses -z output); a listing over maxBytes fails rather than being cut, and createRepoIgnoreFilter treats that failure as 'git failed' and degrades to the permissive filter, as it does for any git failure today

edgeCases.input: The corpus reader asks for many revs at once, including a missing one
edgeCases.expected: git_cat_file with the revs array returns one entry per rev with found=false for the missing one; the reader keeps its per-rev validation results and error codes

edgeCases.input: A site calls git while the work tree is mid-merge or mid-squash (MERGE_HEAD or SQUASH_MSG present)
edgeCases.expected: mergeInProgress returns true through git_rev_parse {verify} on MERGE_HEAD and a read of the git path SQUASH_MSG, exactly as the two execFileSync calls do today

edgeCases.input: gh is not signed in or the installed gh lacks `auth status --json`
edgeCases.expected: identity.ts uses gh_auth status/hosts and reports the recorded behaviour for the older gh (the one allowed difference in ac4); a signed-out gh gives the same 'unavailable' provider diagnostic

edgeCases.input: A daemon method is called while no approval client is attached and a tool of the site is in the common class under manual or edit-auto mode
edgeCases.expected: The call is denied with 'no-client' and the stage fails with that denial (ac5); under the default auto mode common calls run without asking, so no existing flow starts asking

invariantsToPreserve.text: A tool result that does not match its declared schema is a failure and is never passed on as a value; the helpers do not turn schema-mismatch or conversion-failed into a fallback
A ToolDenied is thrown through every catch-all on the call paths and is caught only at a stage boundary; an ordinary failure keeps the site's old result
The team refresh stays inside REFRESH_DEADLINE_MS = 10 s in total, starts no call after the budget is spent, and the sighting lock-lifetime reasoning that depends on it is unchanged
Each moved function returns the same value, and the same failure result, as before for the same repository state; only its type changes from T to Promise<T>
Nothing that reaches an LLM provider runs in parallel; the new helpers make their calls one after another with sequential awaits
Every tool id agents use today keeps working with the same meaning; any extension of a git tool made by this Story only adds an optional input
The old paths stay exported and unchanged until the last site has moved; the deletion is the final task and the build is green before it

migration.stateBefore: After Story s10 the tracker, the terminal client and the commit-and-push callers go through the registry, but 24 sites in 17 files still run git or gh themselves or call a builtin's execute (forbidden-spawn scan, report mode, 45 sites with the 21 old wrappers): the team module's runGit (sync) and runGitAsync, the synchronous build runners (range-base, story-commits, standalone-record), the validation checks, the repo-ignore filter, the companion header, the convert plan, gates.headFullSha, the corpus reader's createGitRunner, and the identity lookup's runShell calls (analyze bundles c1 and c2). The old github.ts wrappers, runGh, commitAndPushArtifacts and the exec test seam are still exported and unchanged, with the legacy-table and registry-table factory test seams that stand in for them in 32 test files (bundle c3). PolicyReader is synchronous and read by seven production sites and faked synchronously in 44 test files.
migration.stateAfter: No file outside src/daemon/tools, the daemon self-update (src/cli/services/maintenance.ts), src/daemon/installed-commit.ts and src/indexer/index.ts runs git, gh or acli itself or calls a builtin's execute: every site calls a named typed tool through callTool with its own caller, signal and approval mode. The old paths (runGit, runGitAsync, runGh, commitAndPushArtifacts, the github.ts wrappers, createGitRunner, runGitBinary, _setTrackerExecForTests, the legacy table and the registry-table factory seams) no longer exist. The scan runs with --fail in the build chain. PolicyReader is async; the refresh budget is a Deadline with an AbortSignal. The migration record and the session source inventory are regenerated and the full sweep shows no new failure or skipped test against the tree before s9.

migrationSteps.action: Verify the replacement table against the tool input schemas: for each of the 24 sites check that the named tool op carries the options the site uses (git_ls_files cached and others, git_path_history diffFilter A and firstParent, git_cat_file exists and revs, git_status path filter, git_rev_parse verify and short, git_config get); where an optional input is missing, add it to that tool as an additive optional input with its own test, flagged for the tool's owner. Add src/workflow/git-calls.ts with its unit tests. Nothing else changes; the build is green. The gap already found: the git commands src/workflow/runners/build/story-commits.ts runs (diff-tree --root -z, merge-tree --write-tree, hash-object -t tree /dev/null, and rev-parse --git-path SQUASH_MSG in mergeInProgress) have no tool or op: diff-tree and merge-tree are assigned to s8 in the coverage table (src/daemon/tools/builtins/git/coverage.ts) and not built, git_hash_object takes a path only and git_rev_parse has no git-path input. This Story builds them, as s7 did for git_config, git_ls_remote, git_update_ref and git_rm: new read-only tools git_diff_tree and git_merge_tree, an optional type input on git_hash_object and an optional gitPath input on git_rev_parse, each with its own tests, and the s8 coverage table marks the two tools built by s9.

Make the consumers await-ready while the producers are still synchronous: widen PolicyReader to return a value or a Promise, add awaits at its seven production readers and in the injected fakes' call sites, and widen the call sites of the synchronous runners (range-base, story-commits, standalone-record, validation-checks, repo-ignore-filter, companion header, convert plan, gates) so each can accept a Promise. Awaiting a plain value is harmless, so the tree stays green and every task is its own commit

migration.backwardCompat: No external interface changes. The IPC methods, the MCP tools, the tool ids and their inputs and outputs are unchanged; any extension made to a git tool is an additive optional input. Internal TypeScript interfaces change: PolicyReader and the listed workflow functions return Promises, and the exports of the old paths disappear; nothing outside this repository imports them (the IDE fork reaches the daemon only through IPC). Artifacts, commits, tracker records and the policy cache files written by the moved stages are byte-for-byte the same as before, which the parity tests check.

alternativesConsidered.name: Rewrite each site onto the typed git and gh tools, asynchronously, through one small call helper
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Every remaining site calls the named git tool (git_rev_parse, git_ls_files, git_log, git_cat_file, git_config, git_ls_remote, git_fetch, git_for_each_ref, git_remote and so on) through callTool; the synchronous functions among them, and the chain above them, become async.
alternativesConsidered.approach: A new module in the s10 table's style (src/workflow/git-calls.ts, built on run/must/soft and workflowToolDeps of src/workflow/tracker/registry-table.ts) offers one function per operation the sites need (revParse, catFileExists, lsFiles, logFirst, configGet, lsRemote, fetchRefs, forEachRef, remoteUrl, status, checkIgnore) that calls the tool with the site's cwd, abort signal and approval mode and returns the plain value the site used (a string, a boolean, a list) or the site's old failure value. Each site keeps its own error policy: an ordinary failure gives the site's old fallback, a ToolDenied is thrown through every catch-all and caught only at the stage boundary (the s10 rule). The team module's two runners are replaced: the policy reader, the anchor finder, the sighting store, the signoff branch checks and the handoff checks call the helpers; the refresh passes one shared deadline as a per-call timeoutMs and one AbortSignal that the 10 s deadline aborts. PolicyReader becomes async (Promise<PolicyResult>), with the type widened to accept both forms during the change and narrowed at the end. The corpus reader's createGitRunner is replaced by git_cat_file with the revs array (git cat-file --batch) and git_ls_tree/git_show; identity.ts calls gh_auth and gh_tracker ops instead of runShell. Then runGit, runGitAsync, runGh, commitAndPushArtifacts, the github.ts wrappers, createGitRunner, _setTrackerExecForTests, the legacy-table test seam and the registry-table factory seam are deleted, and the scan is switched to failing mode.
pros: Each site states which tool it uses, so the replacement table, the migration record and the site-list test can name a row per site (ac1, ac6).
The approval, abort and result-check rules apply to every call with no argv parsing in between (ac1, ac5).
Same pattern as s10, which is built and tested, so the reviewers and the next maintainer find one convention.
cons: The async cascade is wide: PolicyReader and about forty functions above the synchronous sites change signature, and 44 test files that inject a synchronous PolicyReader are touched.
Some operations may have no exact tool op (check-ignore, a config read with a scope); each gap needs an s9-owned additive extension of a git tool, as s10 did for git_push configured.

alternativesConsidered.name: Keep the call shapes: one argv-compatible adapter over the tools
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: A single gitViaTools(cwd, argv, opts) returns the old GitRun shape and maps the known argv forms to tools, so the sites change only at the call line.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add gitViaTools with the signature of runGit/runGitAsync (cwd, argv, timeout or Deadline) that matches argv against a table of the forms the sites use (rev-parse --verify, ls-tree, show, status --porcelain, ls-remote, fetch and so on) and calls the matching tool, returning {ok, stdout} / {ok:false, stderr, quiet|timedOut} built from the tool result. Sites keep their code; only the import changes. An argv with no table entry is refused with a clear error so a new site cannot run git around the registry.
pros: The smallest diff at each site and the smallest change to the existing tests, which already stub the runner by argv.
The result shape (quiet, timedOut) stays as the sites read it today.
cons: It re-creates a second, string-matching layer between the sites and the tools: argv forms drift from the tool inputs, and an unmapped form fails at run time instead of at compile time.

It does not remove the synchronous callers: the sync runGit users still need a synchronous result, which the asynchronous tools cannot give, so the adapter has to be async anyway and the cascade of a1 remains.
The replacement table would list argv strings, not tools, so ac1 (a registry tool called through callTool, with the site setting the caller, signal and approval mode) is met only indirectly.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: It adds an argv-matching layer that is a shim in the sense of k6, scores partial on ac1, ac2, ac6 and ac7, and still needs the same async cascade as a1.

alternativesConsidered.name: Serve the team policy from a daemon-held snapshot and keep PolicyReader synchronous
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: A daemon-side cache of the policy per repo, filled by the tools and refreshed on team.refresh and on a git event, lets the synchronous readers stay synchronous.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add a policy snapshot store in the daemon (per repo: the resolved policy or 'none', the ref and sha it came from, when it was read) filled by an async reader that uses the git tools. PolicyReader stays (repo) => PolicyResult and returns the snapshot, reading it from the store; if there is none yet it returns a 'not read yet' failure that the callers already treat as a refusal. The refresh and a file watcher on .git refs update the snapshot. The other sites move as in a1.
pros: The seven synchronous PolicyReader consumers and the 44 test fakes do not change signature.
A policy read costs no subprocess on the hot path of the claim and approval gates.
cons: It changes behaviour: a read after a local commit or branch switch can return a stale policy until the snapshot refreshes, against ac2 (same results as before) and the DEF's team-mode guarantees; the invalidation rules are a new design.
It adds a store and a watcher that nothing asked for, and the CLI and tests would need a daemon to read a policy.
The anchor finder, the sighting store and the signoff and handoff checks still need async git, so the cascade is only partly avoided.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: It violates ac2: a policy read after a local change can differ from today's until the snapshot refreshes, and it adds a store and a watcher nobody asked for while the other sites still go async.

openQuestions: Decision needed: the git commands src/workflow/runners/build/story-commits.ts runs (diff-tree --root -z, merge-tree --write-tree, hash-object -t tree /dev/null, and rev-parse --git-path SQUASH_MSG in mergeInProgress) have no tool or op: diff-tree and merge-tree are assigned to s8 in the coverage table (src/daemon/tools/builtins/git/coverage.ts) and not built, git_hash_object takes a path only and git_rev_parse has no git-path input. This Story builds them, as s7 did for git_config, git_ls_remote, git_update_ref and git_rm: new read-only tools git_diff_tree and git_merge_tree, an optional type input on git_hash_object and an optional gitPath input on git_rev_parse, each with its own tests, and the s8 coverage table marks the two tools built by s9. The alternative is to build s8 first (its long-tail tools) and let this Story depend on it; the recommended route is the first, so the cutover is not held up by the 93-command long tail.

Which exact tool ops lack an input a site needs (git_status path filter, git_log or git_path_history options for story-commits, git_config scope)? Task t1 of the plan checks every row against the tool input schemas and adds any missing optional input as an additive extension flagged for the tool's owner.
Does any caller of PolicyReader need the opts.signal, or can the signal be dropped from the type to keep the 44 injected fakes' signature unchanged? The default is to keep it optional.
The nine migration steps are written at the level of the area moved and are not the plan's task list; the plan stage decides the tasks and their order.
